content: Sterols, also known as steroid alcohols, are a specific subgroup of steroids characterized by the presence of a hydroxyl group attached to the 3-position of the A-ring in their molecular structure. These molecules are amphipathic lipids, meaning they contain both hydrophilic (water-attracting) and hydrophobic (water-repelling) regions. They are synthesized from acetyl-coenzyme A, a key molecule in metabolic pathways. Structurally, sterols are relatively flat molecules. The hydroxyl group on the A-ring is polar, while the remainder of the aliphatic chain is non-polar. Sterols derived from plants are referred to as phytosterols, while those from animals are called zoosterols. Among the zoosterols, cholesterol and certain steroid hormones are the most significant. In the case of phytosterols, the most important examples include campesterol, sitosterol, and stigmasterol. Sterols play critical roles in the physiology of eukaryotic organisms. For instance, cholesterol is an integral component of cellular membranes, where it influences membrane fluidity and functions as a secondary messenger in developmental signaling pathways. Plant sterols, on the other hand, are known to inhibit cholesterol absorption in the human intestine, thereby contributing to the reduction of cholesterol levels in the body. In humans, sterols are involved in essential signaling and metabolic communication processes. These include regulating circadian rhythms and facilitating blood clotting, among other physiological functions.
